In response to these challenges, Japanese research insti­
tutions proposed the concept of a cloud infrastructure called 
mdx. This infrastructure is collaboratively procured and 
managed by nine national universities and two research 
institutes, delivering services to academic and research 
organizations as well as private sector entities throughout 
Japan. The initial realization of the mdx concept, referred 
to as mdx I [17], was deployed at the University of Tokyo 
and commenced user services in September 2021. To ensure 
uninterrupted operation during maintenance or system 
upgrades, and to enhance resilience against disasters and 
system failures, a second-generation mdx system, named 
mdx II, was established at the University of Osaka (Fig. 1) 
and began operation in November 2024.
Introduction
Recent progress in data collection and analytical technolo­
gies has resulted in the broad integration of data-driven 
methods into scientific research. Consequently, the aca­
demic community is experiencing a growing need for 
computational infrastructure that supports the aggregation, 
storage, and analysis of extensive datasets. Nevertheless,

Abstract
mdx II is an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) cloud developed to accelerate data science research and promote interdis­
ciplinary collaboration among Japanese universities and research organizations. In contrast to conventional high-perfor­
mance computing (HPC) systems, mdx II utilizes OpenStack to deliver flexible, isolated computing resources, including 
virtual machines, virtual networks, and storage systems. This article provides a thorough performance assessment of 
mdx II, benchmarking it against public cloud and bare metal server. We analyzed the performance of a 16-vCPU virtual 
machine in several aspects: floating-point computation, memory bandwidth, network throughput, file system and object 
storage access performance, and real-world application performance. When compared to an AWS 16-vCPU instance, 
mdx II was found to excel in many aspects, highlighting its strong potential for high-performance data analytics (HPDA) 
workloads. Additionally, we investigated the effects of virtualization overhead using a 224-vCPU virtual machine that 
fully occupies a physical host. The results revealed that virtualization overhead is negligible for compute-bound tasks, 
but more pronounced for memory-intensive workloads. We also evaluated the performance of a virtual machine equipped 
with GPUs and demonstrated that the impact of virtualization on GPU performance is negligible. These insights are 
anticipated to help mdx II users in achieving optimal performance for data science tasks and to guide the development of 
future data-centric cloud infrastructures.

mdx II functions as an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) 
cloud platform specifically designed for data science 
research. In contrast to conventional High-Performance 
Computing (HPC) systems, which rely on batch job sched­
ulers and operate on bare metal servers, mdx II is built upon 
the OpenStack cloud computing framework. This architec­
ture enables users to configure isolated, customizable com­
puting environments composed of virtual machines, virtual 
storage, and virtual networks, thereby accommodating a 
wide range of computational, storage, and networking needs. 
Additionally, mdx II supports multiple storage options and 
access protocols, facilitating data ingestion through block 
storage, parallel file systems, and object storage, which are 
accessible via Lustre, the S3 API, and a web interface.
While the hardware components of mdx II share similari­
ties with traditional supercomputers, its software environ­
ment and intended applications differ markedly. Therefore, 
in this article, we conduct an extensive performance assess­
ment of mdx II to inform both current and prospective users 
about the expected system performance characteristics and 
to offer recommendations for optimizing High-Performance 
Data Analytics (HPDA) workloads on the platform. Fur­
thermore, insights gained from the performance analysis are 
intended to provide valuable feedback to system operators 
and to inform the design and configuration of future data-
centric cloud infrastructure.
This article extends our previous conference paper [18] 
by providing an in-depth description of the GPU nodes that 
were deployed to mdx  II after the conference paper was 
published. Moreover, we conduct an extensive performance 
analysis that examines basic performance characteristics of 
the GPU, such as floating-point computing performance, 
memory throughput, inter-GPU communication throughput, 
as well as the performance of real-world machine learning 
and HPC workloads.
The remainder of this article is organized as follows. 
“Background” provides an overview of the mdx II system 
architecture and compares it with other academic cloud 
infrastructures. “Performance Analysis” presents a detailed 
performance evaluation and analysis of mdx  II. Finally, 
“Conclusions and Future Work” summarizes the findings 
and outlines directions for future research.
Background
Overview of mdx II
Figure 2 presents a summary of the mdx II system architec­
ture. Note that mdx II is being incrementally extended, and 
here we describe its latest status as of writing this article. 
The mdx II system as of August 2025 consists of 60 CPU 
nodes and 7 GPU nodes. Each CPU node is equipped with 
two Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (Sapphire Rapids) CPUs, 
512 GiB of DDR5-4800 SDRAM, and a 200 Gbps Ether­
net NIC. Each CPU node delivers a peak double-precision 
floating-point performance of 7,168  GFLOP/s at a base 
clock of 2.0  GHz and offers a maximum memory band­
width of 614 GB/s. Of the total 60 nodes, 54 are orches­
trated by the Red Hat OpenStack Platform (RHOSP),1 while 
the remaining 6 are managed by VMware vSphere. These 
vSphere-managed nodes, referred to as interoperability

The GPU nodes are equipped with two Intel Xeon Gold 
6530 (Emerald Rapids) CPUs, 1024  GiB of DDR5-4800 
SDRAM, and four NVIDIA H200 SXM5 GPUs. The four 
H200 GPUs are directly connected to every other through 
NVLink 4.0, which provides a total of 300 GB/s bidirec­

delivers a peak double-precision floating-point computing 
performance of 34 TFLOP/s, and 4.8 TB/s of memory band­
width. The GPU memory capacity is 141 GB. Each CPU 
is connected to two GPUs and a 200 Gbps Ethernet NIC 
via PCI Express Gen5 x16, delivering 64 GB/s. Each GPU 
is exclusively assigned to a single VM and is connected to 
the VM via PCI Passthrough, bypassing the host kernel. 
Because the GPUs are not virtualized, their performance 
should closely match that of physical GPU servers.
The compute nodes have access to two distinct storage 
systems. The first is a DDN EXAScaler all-NVMe Lustre 
parallel file system with a capacity of 1106 TB. The second 
is a Cloudian HyperStore S3-compatible object storage sys­
tem, offering 432 TB of storage.
Figure  3 illustrates the various access methods avail­
able for the Lustre file system. The primary function of 
the Lustre file system is to serve as a repository for VM 
disk images (① in Fig. 3). Specifically, the directory stor­
ing the VM disk images on Lustre is mounted on a Lustre-
NFS gateway server, which then exports the directory as an 
NFS volume for mounting on each compute node. Each VM 
attaches a disk image file on the NFS volume as a virtual 
disk. During our preliminary testing, we found that access­
ing disk image files through the Lustre-NFS gateway rarely 
resulted in silent data corruption, due to a bug in the Lustre 
client’s page cache management. This issue is being investi­
gated and addressed as of writing this article. As an interim 
solution, we found a way to directly mount the Lustre file 
system on each compute node (② in Fig. 3), thereby bypass­
ing the Lustre-NFS gateway. However, this setup is not offi­
cially supported by RHOSP and should only be considered 
a temporary workaround. Additionally, the Lustre file sys­
tem can be directly mounted by multiple VMs (③ in Fig. 3), 
enabling high-performance parallel I/O by multiple VMs. 
Lastly, the Lustre file system is accessible via the S3 pro­
tocol using S3 Data Services (S3DS), a Lustre-S3 gateway 
provided by DDN (④), as well as through a web interface

In terms of storage, mdx  I offers both SSD-based and 
HDD-based Lustre file systems, as well as S3-compatible 
object storage. The design of mdx I prioritizes robust net­
work isolation among tenants and high communication effi­
ciency. Specifically, mdx I employs Virtual eXtensible LAN 
(VXLAN) for tenant isolation, Single Root I/O Virtualiza­
tion (SR-IOV) to directly connect host NICs to VMs while 
bypassing the hypervisor, and RDMA over Converged 
Ethernet (RoCE) to ensure low-latency, high-throughput 
communication between VMs or between VMs and storage 
systems.
Although mdx I, mdx II, and Jetstream pursue analogous 
objectives, comprehensive performance analyses of these 
platforms remain unavailable. Beyond limited performance 
data collected during system acceptance testing [15], there 
have been no thorough evaluations, published real-world 
benchmarks, or systematic comparisons with public clouds 
to date. Consequently, this article undertakes a detailed 
evaluation and analysis of mdx II, a cutting-edge academic 
cloud infrastructure, aiming to elucidate its performance 
characteristics and potential bottlenecks, thereby informing 
the design of future academic cloud infrastructures.
Performance Analysis
Evaluation Method
Similar to public clouds, mdx  II provides users with the 
flexibility to select the number of vCPUs per VM, with 
options currently spanning from 1 up to 224 vCPUs. Given 
that evaluating every possible VM configuration is unrealis­
tic, we first concentrate on VMs with 16 vCPUs. This choice 
is because the smallest vCPU quota that can be purchased 
on mdx II is presently 16, and such VM sizes are anticipated 
to be commonly used by users. Subsequently, we focus 
on a VM configured with 224 vCPUs, which occupies an 
entire CPU node. This configuration enables a direct perfor­
mance comparison between a VM and a bare metal server 
equipped with equivalent hardware. Lastly, we focus on a 
VM equipped with GPUs to compare its performance with 
that of a bare metal server and public cloud.
16-vCPU VM
For the evaluation, we select the mdx  II vc16m32g 
instance type, which provides 16 vCPUs and 32  GiB of 
memory. As a baseline, we utilize Amazon Web Services 
(AWS), a well-known public cloud provider. In particular, 
the c7i.4xlarge instance type is chosen, as it is based 
on the same CPU generation (Sapphire Rapids) as mdx II 
built on Nextcloud.2 Physically, the Lustre storage consists 
of two DDN ES400NVX2 appliances, each equipped with 
24 NVMe SSDs of 30 TB capacity.
The S3-compatible object storage is integrated with the 
SQUID supercomputer [3] at the University of Osaka and 
is connected to mdx II via a 10 Gbps Ethernet link. This 
object storage cluster comprises six Cloudian HyperStore 
HSA-1610 appliances configured with a 4+2 erasure coding 
scheme, whereby each object is divided into four data frag­
ments and two parity fragments, distributed across different 
object storage nodes.
All compute nodes, Lustre storage nodes, and servers 
are interconnected by a 200 Gbps Ethernet network. Two 
overlay networks are implemented on top of the physical 
network. The first overlay network, which employs Generic 
Network Virtualization Encapsulation (Geneve) [7], serves 
as the primary virtual network for both CPU and GPU VMs. 
The second overlay network employs Virtual LAN (VLAN) 
and enables high-speed communication exclusively among 
GPU VMs. Through Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-
IOV) [11], GPU VMs are able to access this VLAN net­
work directly, bypassing the host kernel and thus potentially 
achieving higher network performance. For external con­
nectivity, the system is connected to a Japanese academic 
network, Science Information NETwork (SINET), and the 
internet via the University of Osaka’s campus network.
Related Work
Jetstream [16] represents the first operational cloud infra­
structure within the NSF-funded Extreme Science and Engi­
neering Discovery Environment (XSEDE) [19], specifically 
developed to facilitate interactive computing for research­
ers whose requirements do not align with conventional HPC 
paradigms. Built on OpenStack, Jetstream enables users to 
deploy VMs and integrates authentication and data transfer 
capabilities via Globus. Expanding upon this foundation, 
Jetstream 2 [8] was introduced as the next generation of the 
Jetstream infrastructure, incorporating heterogeneous hard­
ware resources such as GPUs, software-defined storage, 
and container orchestration capabilities. The main Jetstream 
2 installation resides at Indiana University,3 comprising 
384 compute nodes, 32 large-memory nodes, and 90 GPU 
nodes. The system utilizes AMD EPYC 7713 (Milan) pro­
cessors and NVIDIA A100 SXM4 40 GB GPUs.
mdx I [17], the precursor to mdx II, is deployed at the 
University of Tokyo. This system consists of 368 CPU 
nodes and 40 GPU nodes, featuring Intel Xeon Platinum 
8368 (IceLake-SP) CPUs and NVIDIA A100 40 GB GPUs.

Network Performance
To evaluate the network performance of a VM, we utilize 
iPerf version 3.185 to measure the TCP throughput between 
VMs located either on the same compute node or on sepa­
rate compute nodes. Since a single TCP stream is insufficient 
to fully utilize the 200 Gbps physical network bandwidth, 
we generate multiple parallel TCP streams. The zero-copy 
option (-Z) in iPerf is also enabled, leveraging the send­
file() system call in place of write() to reduce CPU 
overhead and enhance throughput.
Figure  4 illustrates the measured throughput between 
two VMs as the number of TCP streams varies. For VMs 
residing on the same node, the single-stream throughput 
reaches 31.6 Gbps, whereas VMs on different nodes achieve 
a throughput of 12.9 Gbps. Increasing the number of par­
allel TCP streams does not, however, lead to a substantial 
improvement in either intra-node or inter-node throughput. 
This limitation can be explained from the architecture of the 
virtio-net/vhost-net [1] paravirtualized NIC employed in 
OpenStack. Figure 5 illustrates the architecture of the virtio-
net/vhost-net paravirtualized NIC. The paravirtualized NIC 
is mainly composed of the virtio-net frontend driver running 
inside the guest kernel, and the vhost-net backend driver 
running inside the host kernel. virtio-net and vhost-net com­
municate via a queue shared between the guest and host ker­
nels. When the guest transmits a packet, virtio-net forwards 
it to vhost-net via the shared queue. vhost-net then transmits 
the packet using the host network stack. By default, virtio-
net/vhost-net creates only a single queue for communication 
between the guest and host kernels, resulting in serialized 
packet transmissions. As a result, the overall throughput

Computing Performance
To assess floating-point computing performance, we 
employ the Intel-optimized High-Performance LIN­
PACK (HPL) Benchmark provided in the Intel oneAPI 
HPC Toolkit 2025.0.1. Memory throughput is evaluated 
using BabelStream4 version 5.0, which is compiled with 
the Intel oneAPI DPC++/C++ Compiler and the flags-
O3,-march=native,-qopt-zmm-usage=high, 
and-qopt-streaming-stores=always.
Table 1 presents a comparison of HPL performance and 
memory throughput between mdx II and AWS. The HPL 
benchmark on mdx  II achieves 1.34  TFLOPS, which is 
double the performance observed on AWS. This disparity is 
likely due to the absence of vCPU pinning on mdx II, allow­
ing vCPUs to run on separate physical cores. In contrast, 
AWS implements vCPU pinning to logical cores, thereby 
reducing interference between instances; as a result, two 
vCPUs are assigned to each physical core on AWS, leading 
to half the performance compared to mdx II. Additionally, 
the mdx II VM delivers 1.7× greater memory throughput, 
which may also be attributed to weaker resource isolation.

200 Gbps link bandwidth. To further explore scalability, we 
examine whether higher total throughput can be achieved 
when multiple VMs concurrently generate multiple TCP 
streams.
Figure 7 depicts the aggregate TCP throughput between 
several pairs of VMs located either on the same compute 
node or on separate nodes, with each VM generating 16 TCP 
streams. The results show that total inter-node throughput 
increases linearly with up to three VMs, eventually plateau­
ing at 126 Gbps. We attribute the discrepancy between the 
observed throughput and the 200 Gbps host NIC bandwidth 
to various overheads associated with virtual networking.
To assess the impact of virtio multiqueue on network 
latency, we utilize netperf6 version 2.7.0, employing the 
TCP_RR test, which repeatedly exchanges requests and 
responses over TCP to measure round-trip latency. Figure 8 
displays the latency measurements. The average round-trip 
latency between VMs on the same node is 55 µs, regardless 
of whether multiqueue is enabled, indicating no observable 
latency overhead. For VMs on different nodes, the mean 
round-trip latency is 74 µs without multiqueue and 85 µs 
with multiqueue. Given the substantial throughput improve­
ments provided by virtio multiqueue, we consider the 15% 
increase in latency to be an acceptable trade-off.
In conclusion, mdx II is capable of delivering network 
throughput of up to 80 Gbps to VMs, surpassing most pub­
lic clouds. However, this level of performance is attainable 
only when virtio multiqueue is activated. Consequently, we 
recommend that mdx II operators enable virtio multiqueue 
by default.

File System Performance
Given that data science applications frequently exhibit I/O-
bound characteristics [12], the performance of the underly­
ing file system is a critical factor for cloud infrastructure. 
In this context, we evaluate and compare the throughput 
and IOPS of mdx II block storage, mdx II Lustre storage, 
and AWS block storage. The Flexible I/O tester (fio)7 ver­
sion 3.38 is employed to assess file access performance. To 
ensure the I/O stack is fully exercised, we utilize the libaio 
asynchronous I/O backend (–ioengine=libaio) and 
configure a substantial number of concurrent in-flight I/O 
requests (–iodepth=256). To eliminate the influence 
of the page cache, the O_DIRECT option (–direct=1) 
is enabled, thereby bypassing the page cache. For AWS, 
we select the General Purpose SSD (gp3) volume type.

In summary, mdx II block storage demonstrates superior 
performance compared to AWS, particularly in terms of read 
operations. Moreover, Lustre storage provides significantly 
higher throughput and IOPS than block storage. It should be 
noted that this evaluation was conducted immediately after 
the launch of the mdx II service when system utilization 
was still low. Therefore, the I/O performance might become 
lower due to contention and interference when the system is 
highly utilized.
Object Storage Performance
Object storage services, such as AWS Simple Storage Ser­
vice (S3), have become prevalent as data lakes, and a wide 
range of data science libraries and frameworks now support 
direct data access from S3-compatible storage. To assess

In conclusion, the performance of Cloudian HyperStore 
is constrained by the limited bandwidth connecting it to the 
mdx II compute nodes. Therefore, for workloads demanding 
high S3 access performance, Cloudian HyperStore should 
be avoided. In such scenarios, it is advisable to stage data 
on DDN S3DS instead.
Data Science Application Performance
To evaluate the practical performance of mdx  II for data 
science applications, we focus on Python-based workloads, 
Figure  13 illustrates the throughput results for DDN 
S3DS. For a single client, the PUT throughput is 227 MiB/s 
and the GET throughput is 898 MiB/s, representing a 3–4× 
improvement over HyperStore. As the number of clients 
increases, GET performance rises substantially, reaching 
9444  MiB/s with 128 clients. This value approaches the 
maximum achievable network throughput, suggesting that 
the guest network is the primary bottleneck. In contrast, 
PUT throughput plateaus at 1435 MiB/s with 16 clients and 
does not increase with additional clients. The underlying 
causes for the limited scalability and lower performance of 
PUT operations compared to GET operations are not yet 
fully understood. We intend to explore the factors affecting

Table 2 presents a summary of the measured computing 
and memory performance. The benchmarking methodology 
matches that used for the 16 vCPU scenario described in 
“Computing Performance”. The results indicate that virtual­
ization introduces only minimal overhead to floating-point 
computing performance. However, a noticeable reduction is 
observed in memory throughput: the mdx II VM achieves 
383 GB/s, which is 22% lower than the bare metal server. 
One potential reason behind the substantial decrease is 
the absence of vCPU pinning in mdx II. Without pinning, 
vCPUs are allowed to migrate freely between the two CPU 
sockets, leading to increased cross-socket memory traffic 
and reduced effective memory throughput. Another poten­
tial reason is that mdx II does not enable Huge Pages, a fea­
ture that allows using a page size larger than the default. 
Although Huge Pages could reduce the overhead of translat­
ing from guest virtual addresses to host physical addresses, 
it is not enabled in mdx II due to drawbacks including mem­
ory fragmentation.

Network Performance
As described in “Overview of mdx II”, GPU VMs in mdx II 
can be directly connected to the physical NICs using SR-
IOV, bypassing the host kernel. In this evaluation, we mea­
sure the network performance of a GPU VM with SR-IOV 
enabled to assess the performance benefit of SR-IOV. Fig­
ure 17 compares the total TCP throughput between two CPU 
VMs or two GPU VMs measured using iPerf. Evidently, SR-
IOV dramatically improves the TCP throughput. The single-
stream throughput increases by fourfold from 11.1 Gbps to 
44.3 Gbps. The maximum throughput is 178 Gbps, which is 
achieved with 16 TCP streams and is 2.2× higher than the 
default network.

VMs measured using netperf. The mean round-trip latency 
is 28 µs, which is 2.6× lower than the default network. Fur­
thermore, the standard deviation is reduced by 5.5×, indicat­
ing significantly smaller packet jitter. Overall, the SR-IOV 
network offers higher bandwidth, lower latency and jitter.

Conclusions and Future Work
Our evaluation of the mdx II cloud infrastructure revealed 
that it consistently outperforms AWS across several key met­
rics, including floating-point computation, memory band­
width, and storage I/O performance. These results establish 
mdx II as an IaaS cloud well-suited for high-performance 
data analytics (HPDA) workloads, especially given its 
advanced storage solutions such as Lustre. Although virtu­
alization overhead is more pronounced in memory-bound 
applications, its negligible effect on compute-focused 
benchmarks demonstrates mdx II’s ability to efficiently sup­
port a broad spectrum of HPC and HPDA use cases.
Future work will involve the analysis and optimization 
of large-scale, real-world data science workloads on mdx II, 
further strengthening its role in accelerating data science 
research and fostering interdisciplinary collaboration. Addi­
tionally, we plan to investigate the energy efficiency and 
cost-effectiveness of mdx II relative to other academic and 
commercial cloud platforms.

Abstract: mdx II is an Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) cloud developed to accelerate data science research and promote interdis­ ciplinary collaboration among Japanese universities and research organizations. In contrast to conventional high-perfor­ mance computing (HPC) systems, mdx II utilizes OpenStack to deliver flexible, isolated computing resources, including virtual machines, virtual networks, and storage systems. This article provides a thorough performance assessment of mdx II, benchmarking it against public cloud and bare metal server. We analyzed the performance of a 16-vCPU virtual machine in several aspects: floating-point computation, memory bandwidth, network throughput, file system and object storage access performance, and real-world application performance. When compared to an AWS 16-vCPU instance, mdx II was found to excel in many aspects, highlighting its strong potential for high-performance data analytics (HPDA) workloads. Additionally, we investigated the effects of virtualization overhead using a 224-vCPU virtual machine that fully occupies a physical host. The results revealed that virtualization overhead is negligible for compute-bound tasks, but more pronounced for memory-intensive workloads. We also evaluated the performance of a virtual machine equipped with GPUs and demonstrated that the impact of virtualization on GPU performance is negligible. These insights are anticipated to help mdx II users in achieving optimal performance for data science tasks and to guide the development of future data-centric cloud infrastructures.
